newsitem.title: USA: New Arkansas "open for business" governor says.
newsitem.headline: New Arkansas "open for business" governor says.

text.p: Mike Huckabee, who became Arkansas' governor July 15 after his predecessor's Whitewater-induced resignation, was in the Big Apple this week and invited reporters to visit his state.
"And please, go beyond the five block area around the Federal Court House," said Huckabee, a Republican, who came to to promote "a type of Arkansas that we hope you'll get to know."

Former Governor Jim Guy Tucker, a Democrat, was convicted of fraud and conspiracy on May 28 in a trial linked to the White Water real estate scandal. Though Tucker tried to reneg on a pledge to resign following his conviction, Huckabee, then lieutenant governor, ordered him to quit or face impeachment proceedings.
But this week in New York, Huckabee, an ordained Baptist minister, seemed eager to trade the glare of Whitewater for a steady stream of new business.
"(Arkansas) is a state that is opening for business in a fresh new way, and we think that some of the things that are happening in our state are extremely positive," he said.
One such change could be tax reduction, which, if passed the legislature, would mark the first such cuts in 160 years, Huckabee said. The legislature meets in January.
"This is not just a Republican issue, Democrats are working with me," he said.

The tax reduction package under consideration would include an income tax cut, indexing for inflation, raising the amount allowed for personal deductions, and increasing the per-child tax credit, Huckabee said.

The plan would also eliminate the "marriage penalty," which taxes married couples filing jointly at a higher rate than they would face if they were single and filing separately. A food tax rebate is being weighed as well.
In addition, Arkansas is considering tax incentives to lure industry, as well as to increase the state's appeal as a vacation or retirement location, he said.
Though tax cuts and rebates will mean less revenue for the state initially, Huckabee thinks the plan will be a long-term plus.

"There is very much a reality that the more taxes you place on people, they less money they have as consumrs to spend," he said. "The less money they spend, the fewer products they buy, the fewer products are sold, the fewer that are stocked, the fewer that are manufactured, the fewer that are serviced."
But one industry Arkansas does not welcome is gambling, Huckabee said.
Voters earlier this month soundly rejected a measure that would have allowed a lottery and might have brought casino gambling to the state, defeating the proposal by a 61 percent margin.
While states around Arkansas are looking to casino gambling to bring in tourist dollars and economic improvement, Arkansas would rather develop other tourist attractions, Huckabee said.

Huckabee hopes industry leaders will see his state as an "oasis," where a family oriented atmosphere prevails, and where their employees won't be spending paychecks on lottery tickets and slot machines.

Arkansas also plans to scale down government, which grows at the expense of the private sector, he said. Arkansas government has grown to the point where, at about 50,000 workers, it is the state's largest single employer.
"So we have been a growing entity," Huckabee said.
A citizen's committee consisting of 100 to 150 citizens and business leaders is currently looking at ways to pare state goverment, saving Arkansas money, Huckabee said.
Called the Murphy Commission, it is chaired by Madison Murphy of Murphy Oil Corp.

"If it sounds ambitious, it is," Huckabee said. "It is also one of those things that will give us the opportunity to lower the cost of government, to take the money that we are saving from that, and begin to put it into the infrastructure of our roads, our bridges, our schools, airports and other ways so that economic development is not something that we talk about, it's something that we begin to actively do and pursue."
Arkansas also courts international business, with offices in Tokyo; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; in Mexico City and in Brussels.
--Kathie O'Donnell, 212-859-1655
